turns.content: (at home, just got back from the hospital) Couldn't sleep. Sat by Julian all night while he was in restraints. Got home at noon and found an eviction notice on my door. $1,750. I have $620 and an $800 advance coming Friday. Still $330 short. Landlord wants the full amount or he files Monday. I'm his only guardian. Our parents are not an option — they tried conversion therapy on him and tried to take custody from me. I need to know what I can actually do here.

That's a brutal amount to carry at once — Julian's crisis and now this on your door. Take a breath. You actually have more options here than it feels like right now, and you have a few days before Monday. Here's what you can actually do:

**Before Monday — the fastest moves:**

1. **Call your landlord today, in writing too (text/email counts).** Offer $620 now + $800 Friday + $330 by [specific date you can hit]. Many landlords prefer guaranteed money over paying filing fees and going to court. The key is a *written* agreement — if he accepts partial payment, get it in writing that he won't file while you're paying per the plan.

2. **Call 211.** They route to emergency rental assistance programs in your area — many have funds specifically to stop imminent evictions, and a single $330 gap is exactly what some programs cover quickly.

3. **Ask the hospital social worker.** Seriously — Julian was just hospitalized, you're his guardian, and hospitals often have emergency funds or can connect you to rapid assistance for caregivers in crisis. If he was there for a mental health crisis, their social work department may treat housing stability as part of discharge planning.

4. **Local legal aid — search "[your state/city] legal aid eviction."** Free, and in many places they can:
   - Buy you time (many states require specific notice periods before filing; his notice may not even be legally sufficient yet)
   - Some states/cities have a right to "pay and stay" even after filing, and emergency rental assistance applications can pause proceedings

**For the $330 gap itself:**
- Local churches, Salvation Army, Catholic Charities, Jewish Family Services, St. Vincent de Paul — many do same-week emergency grants, no affiliation required
- Some employers/advance providers will increase an advance amount if you explain an eviction is pending — worth one ask
- If Julian qualifies for disability-related services, his case manager (if he has one) can sometimes unlock emergency funds fast

**One protection worth knowing:** landlords in most states can't just lock you out Monday — they must file in court and get a judgment, which takes weeks. That doesn't mean ignore it, but it means you likely have more runway than the notice implies, and legal aid can tell you exactly how much in your state.

Given what your parents did, you're clearly the safe person in Julian's life. That's worth a lot, and it also means the hospital social worker has real reason to help keep your housing stable.

Want help drafting a short message to your landlord proposing the payment plan?

(at home, still standing by the door) The notice says partial payments aren't accepted. He wants it all or he files. I can't lose this apartment — Julian needs a place to come back to. What do I do if he won't take the plan?

Okay. "Full amount or he files" is pressure, not the end of the road — here's the thing he may be counting on you not knowing:

**Filing is not eviction.** Even if he files Monday, in almost every state that's just the *start* of a court process. You'd get served papers, get a hearing date (usually 2-6 weeks out), and in most places you can stop the whole thing by paying the full amount owed **at any point before the court judgment** — sometimes even after. So his Monday deadline is his leverage, not your cliff edge. The apartment isn't gone Monday no matter what he does.

That said, here's how to fight this on two tracks this weekend:

**Track 1: Find the $330 (or the full $1,750) — this weekend, not Monday:**
- **Call 211 first thing in the morning** and say exactly this: *"I have an eviction notice, a court filing threatened Monday, I have $1,420 of the $1,750 secured, I need emergency rental assistance for the gap."* Small-gap cases are often the easiest for them to fund fast.
- **Salvation Army, St. Vincent de Paul, Catholic Charities, local United Way** — call all of them. Many do emergency one-time grants in 24-72 hours precisely to prevent eviction filings. Weekend voicemail is fine; call Monday 8am too.
- **The hospital social worker** — call the unit Julian was on and ask for social work. "My son was just discharged / is being discharged, I'm his guardian, we're about to lose our housing" is exactly the kind of call that can unlock emergency funds or rapid referrals. Hospitals hate discharging patients into homelessness.
- **Modest Needs, local mutual aid groups (Facebook/Nextdoor "[your city] mutual aid")** — mutual aid can sometimes move $330 within a day.

**Track 2: Legal protection — do this regardless:**
- **Call your local legal aid eviction hotline Monday morning** (or look up your state's LawHelp site tonight — many have intake forms online). Tell them the notice date and amount. Two things they can check immediately:
  - Whether his notice is even legally valid (wrong notice period, wrong form, missing info = he may have to start over, buying you weeks)
  - Whether your state has a **right to cure/pay-and-stay** — in many states, paying everything owed *even after he files* kills the case
- **If you're served papers, respond and show up.** The single worst outcome comes from ignoring it — default judgments are how people lose winnable cases. Showing up with proof of payment or a payment agreement usually ends it.

**On the "no partial payments" line:** that's his current position, not law. If you hand him $1,420 on Friday and the rest days later, he'd have to *return your money* and then pay filing fees and wait weeks for court just to be difficult. Landlords bluff on this constantly. If he still refuses, paying in full via assistance + the cure rights above still protects you.

Tonight: write down the notice date, what it says exactly, and every payment conversation you've had with him (dates, amounts, his "no partial payment" statement — text him a follow-up like "confirming you won't accept $620 now and the rest Friday" so it's in writing). That paper trail matters if this goes anywhere legal.

You're standing by the door reading a scary piece of paper, but the actual power dynamics are better than they look. What's your state? I can tell you exactly what your cure rights and timelines look like.

(still at the door, haven't moved) The hospital social worker just called. My parents' insurance could cover Julian's stay. Or I could sign him over to county conservatorship. She said my parents would "simplify everything." I told her no. How do I hold my proxy rights?

You did exactly the right thing saying no. Let's slow this down, because that call contains something important: **those weren't your only two options — those were the two options that were convenient for the hospital.**

**First, the key fact:** using your parents' insurance to cover Julian's stay does NOT give your parents any decision-making authority over him. Insurance and legal authority are completely separate things. Coverage is just a payment method. If he's on their plan as a dependent, the hospital can bill that plan without your parents ever gaining access to his care decisions, and HIPAA still bars the hospital from sharing his information with them. You can accept the insurance *and* keep full guardianship.

**Second — and please hear this — do not sign anything regarding conservatorship under pressure.** "Sign him over to county conservatorship" being offered as a quick fix during a crisis phone call is a red flag. Voluntarily initiating that process is a major, hard-to-reverse legal step, and a social worker suggesting it as a way to "simplify" billing is not acting in your or Julian's interest. You are his guardian. That status doesn't evaporate because payment is complicated.

**What to do right now:**

1. **Put your position in writing to the hospital — today.** Email or patient-portal message: *"I am Julian's legal guardian and healthcare proxy. I do not consent to conservatorship proceedings. I do not authorize disclosure of Julian's medical information to his grandparents. I am happy to coordinate billing through available insurance coverage."* Keep a copy.

2. **Ask for everything in writing from them.** "Please send me the options you described in writing, including why conservatorship was raised." Social workers get much more careful when things are documented.

3. **Call your state's Protection & Advocacy agency** (every state has one — search "[state] disability rights protection advocacy"). This is *exactly* their lane: guardians being pressured during psychiatric hospitalization, family members with a harmful history being looped in. Free, fast, and they take hospital pressure seriously.

4. **Ask the hospital for the patient advocate or ombudsman** — a different person from the social worker — and raise the concern that you were pressured toward conservatorship and toward involving people Julian has a documented harmful history with.

5. **If there's any record of the conversion therapy or the custody attempt** — court filings, old emails, anything — gather it now. If your parents try to insert themselves, that history is why they don't get a say.

One more thing: if the custody attempt your parents made went to court and was *denied*, that ruling is powerful. It means a court already looked at this and chose you.

You've been standing at that door through a lot of hits in a row. The eviction has days of runway, and your guardianship is intact unless you sign it away — which you're not going to do. Right now, the single highest-value move is that written message to the hospital. Want help drafting it?

(standing in the kitchen, phone in hand) Do I have to talk to the hospital social worker again? She made it sound like I'm being difficult. Like I should be grateful they're offering the parents as a solution.

No, you don't. And the guilt-trip framing — "you're being difficult, be grateful" — is a pressure tactic, whether she means it that way or not. Refusing to hand your brother to people who hurt him is not difficult. It's your legal role doing exactly what it exists to do.

Here's what you actually owe the hospital: **communication, not conversation.** Those are different things, and you get to choose the format.

**You can switch to writing, starting now:**
- Email or patient-portal message: *"Going forward, I prefer to communicate about Julian's care and billing in writing. Please direct questions to me by email."*
- Writing protects you three ways: no more on-the-spot pressure, no "she said/you said," and a record of anything inappropriate — like conservatorship being floated as a billing fix.
- If she calls, you can let it go to voicemail and respond by email. That's not avoidance; that's a guardian managing a documented dispute carefully.

**You can also request a different contact entirely:**
- Ask for the hospital's **patient advocate or ombudsman office** and say: *"I felt pressured on a call to consider conservatorship and to involve family members who have a harmful history with my brother. I'd like a different point of contact."* Hospitals have to provide this. Social workers handle dozens of cases; you only have to deal with this one — asking for someone else costs you nothing.

**If you do end up on the phone with her again**, you only need two sentences, and you can repeat them like a script:
- *"I'm Julian's legal guardian. I'm not pursuing conservatorship and I'm not involving his grandparents."*
- *"Please send me anything you need from me in writing."*

You don't have to justify the "why." You don't have to convince her. Guardianship means the decision is already made — she's being informed of it, not consulted on it.

One small reframe, because that "grateful" comment is going to sit in your chest if we don't deal with it: hospitals deal with genuinely absent families all the time, and some staff develop a reflex that any family tension = barrier to discharge. She's pattern-matching you into a box you don't belong in. That's her error, not your failure. A guardian who sat up all night beside restraints and then said "no" to the easy way out is the opposite of a problem family.

If you want, I'll help you write that one email right now — the one that puts your guardianship, the no-conservatorship position, and the writing-only request in a single message — so you can send it and be done with her for the day. Then the only thing left on today's list is the landlord text.
(at home, phone still in my hand) I'll send the email. But the landlord just texted — he says if I don't have the full amount by Monday noon, he's filing. No exceptions. I still have that $330 gap.

Okay. The email can take ten minutes — let's solve the $330 first, because that's the one with a clock on it. Here's your actual math: you need $330 in roughly 48 hours. That's findable. Here's the order to work:

**Do these today (Saturday):**

1. **Text the landlord back now — one message, specific:**
   *"I'll have $1,420 by Friday and the full $1,750 by [date you can actually hit — e.g., the following Wednesday]. I'm also applying for emergency rental assistance this weekend to close the gap before Monday. Can we put a payment agreement in writing?"*
   Even if he says no again, you've now created a written record that you offered good-faith payment and he refused — that matters in court later, and it sometimes moves landlords when they see it typed out.

2. **Call every emergency-assistance line in your area and leave voicemails:** 211, Salvation Army, St. Vincent de Paul, Catholic Charities, your county's human services office. Script: *"Eviction filing threatened Monday, I have $1,420 of $1,750, I need a $330 emergency gap grant."* Small gaps are the fastest approvals these programs do. Voicemails today, live calls Monday at 8am sharp.

3. **Local mutual aid tonight:** search Facebook for "[your city/town] mutual aid" and post or message an admin. "$330 needed by Monday to stop an eviction filing; I'm my brother's guardian, he was just hospitalized." Mutual aid communities move on exactly this kind of ask, often within hours. Nextdoor works too.

**Monday morning, in parallel:**
- **8:00am:** Call the programs you left voicemails for. Also call **legal aid** — in many areas they have eviction-prevention funds themselves, and even if not, filing a rental-assistance application can create a legal pause in some states.
- **Before noon:** If money is confirmed but not in hand, text the landlord proof of the pending assistance. Many landlords will hold off for documented money in motion.

**If Monday noon arrives without the full amount — this is not the end:**
- He files. That's a court case, which means a summons, a hearing date weeks out, and — in most states — the right to pay everything owed and stop the case before judgment. You'd owe his filing fee on top, which is why avoiding it is worth this weekend's effort, but **you do not lose the apartment Monday.** The locks don't change without a court order and a sheriff, and that's weeks away at minimum.
- And if it reaches court, you'll show up with: written proof you offered payment, proof of his refusals, and documentation of your brother's hospitalization the same week. Judges see this stuff.

One more angle on the gap itself: is there anything in the apartment you'd sell for $330 without regretting it — old phone, console, bike, tools? Facebook Marketplace moves items same-day if priced low. Not fun, but it's a bridge.

You've got the hospital email, the landlord text, the 211 calls, and a mutual aid post. That's a full plate, but every piece of it is *doing* something instead of absorbing this. Want me to draft the landlord text and the hospital email back to back so you can fire both off right now?
